speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPORTATION OF VOLKS-WAGENS BY STUDEBAKER COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday I was questioned with respect to the importation of Volkswagen cars by Studebaker Corporation under the terms of the automotive pact and its predecessor, order in council PC 1963-1/1544. I was asked by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition to table a letter written in this regard by an official of my department.
In so doing let me make it clear that under either of these authorities, and in fact under the authority of the Customs Act and the transfer invoice procedures of very long standing, any person may, before goods are cleared through customs, sell such goods and transfer title to a new owner so that he may become the importer of record. Of course these transactions must be bona fide and supported by the proper customs and other documentation.
In this instance before us inquiries were made by Studebaker as to whether they could carry out such transactions. The answer was "yes", as evidenced by the reply addressed to them by the department, a copy of which, with the consent of the house, I hereby table along with copies of the automotive pact and the related order-in-council, its predecessor order in council and the departmental memorandum and instructions concerning transfer invoices.
The fact that Studebaker could import Volkswagen vehicles free of duty under the automotive pact or its predecessor did not alter this right in any way. Any Canadian manufacturer of motor vehicles who meets the contitions of the relevant tariff items and orders in council has been and is free to import foreign made vehicles of any make.
As hon. members know, the automotive pact is to encourage increased production of motor vehicles and automotive parts in Canada. As part of this plan, which also seeks
rationalization, Canadian manufacturers become entitled to enter vehicles and original equipment parts duty free provided, of course, they meet the conditions under the pact and the related orders in council that entitle them to this free entry.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The house will recall that prior to the automotive pact there was an earlier program which allowed duty free importations of automobiles and parts by a company which earned this right by increasing its exports from Canada of an equivalent value of cars and parts. Studebaker in fact availed itself of the right to import foreign cars on a duty free basis under both the old program and the present program which replaced it.
One of the conditions of the present program which must be met is that the automobile manufacturer in question has to maintain the ratio between his production of automobiles in Canada and his total sales of automobiles in Canada. This condition is spelled out precisely and clearly in a tariff item contained in order in council P.C. 1965-99 dated January 16, 1965 and tabled in the house at the time the automotive pact was under discussion.
This means that if the company chooses to import automobiles from abroad and sell them in Canada it must increase its production in Canada by an amount equivalent to such importations. Studebaker claims to have done this. It can be seen therefore that if Studebaker performed in accordance with the requirements of the relative tariff items it would have raised its total production of cars in Canada, thus creating jobs and providing additional business for Canadian suppliers, which were the central purposes of the automotive program.
Studebaker, a recognized car manufacturer in Canada, which had earned its right to free entry, found itself in the unique position of being unable to import Studebaker cars after the production of their parent company in the United States had ceased. As a result it chose to import other cars, as it was entitled to do because of its greatly expanded manufacturing activities in Canada. It chose to import Volkswagen cars, but before doing so it wrote to the department to ascertain whether it
Oclober 27, 1966

Importation of Volkswagens could purchase and import such cars duty free. As I have pointed out, they were entitled to do so, as any other manufacturer of motor vehicles in Canada would have been, provided they abided by the Customs Tariff, the Customs Act, the relevant orders in council and the established procedures.
The question now is whether or not they in fact did so. This will be established in the course of the departmental audit of their company, to which I have already referred in the house, as it will in the case of all other car manufacturers required to meet not only the terms of the auto pact and related orders in council but also the customs law and established procedures.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is very touchy on this. The statement that he made was this, as I remember it although I do not have Hansard before me; that the investigation started before yesterday. This was the statement he made in the house. They waited a long, long while, and the effect of the explanation given to us that the investigation started before yesterday I would regard as an admission that it commenced within very recent days. An investigation that commenced six months ago or longer certainly would not be described in colloquial language as "before yesterday".
I want to refer to the document which was filed, and I thank the minister for filing it. I am in agreement with the terms under which it was filed. These are the words in this letter dated December 3, 1964 from the assistant deputy minister of national revenue to Mr. Grundy, president of Studebaker of Canada Limited:
Dear Mr. Grundy:
I have your letter of November 30, 1964, enclosing a copy of your communication of the same date to Volkswagen (Canada), Limited, Toronto, in connection with the proposed importation of automotive vehicles from Europe.
It is noted therefrom that you contemplate entering into an arrangement whereby your company will import Volkswagen motor vehicles from Germany duty free under the terms of order in council P.C. 1963-1/1544, dated October 22, 1963, and subsequently sell them to Volkswagen (Canada) Limited, Toronto. You request departmental confirmation that the order permits of such customs clearance. In this connection, I would advise that to the extent to which you possess duty free entry privileges as determined under the order, you may import Volkswagen motor vehicles duty free thereunder.
It is noted, too, that you intend to enter the vehicles on the basis of transfer invoices prepared by Volkswagen (Canada) Limited. On the understanding that the documentation presented at customs represents the true transaction, the transfer invoice procedure may be used, provided of course, the terms of departmental memorandum D44-3, copy herewith, are observed.
In accordance with your request, a copy of this letter is being sent to Mr. K. L. Barths, managing director of Volkswagen (Canada) Limited, Toronto.
If this be the offspring of the Canada-U.S. auto agreement, then indeed it is an offspring of which no government can be proud. What this amounts to is that Volkswagen has been able to bring these automobiles into Canada

10,000 of them, I think-through an opening that is provided in the agreement. Does the Canadian consumer benefit as a result? He does not benefit one bit. The tariff of 17 per cent, or whatever the amount is, goes to Studebaker and not to the people of Canada. This thing is wrong and unjustifiable

Oclober 27, 1966	COMMONS
in every sense of the word. Jobs have been lost to Canadians. The Studebaker Company has been permitted to make a large killing at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer. It has denied jobs to Canadians, and the minister has the collosal effrontery to say it is good for Canada. This is all I have to say at this point.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPORTATION OF VOLKS-WAGENS BY STUDEBAKER COMPANY
speechtext: Importation of Volkswagens of these companies with respect to this kind of transaction. Because, in spite of what the minister said, this transaction will do nothing to increase jobs for Canadian workers. All it has done so far is deprive the Canadian treasury of $2 million, most of which apparently was taken by Studebaker which was not entitled to that money.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPORTATION OF VOLKS-WAGENS BY STUDEBAKER COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement which has just been made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) is indeed contradictory, and I am in full agreement with what has just been said by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), to the effect that this whole transaction, in the final analysis, means only profits for the Studebaker company, which ceased its manufacturing operations in the United States and which the government says still has enough credits to purchase 10,000 Volkswagens and more than 75,000 other automobiles in the future.
The minister tells us also that this authorization given by his department was such as to promote production of cars in Canada. How can production of cars in Canada be promoted when regulations are made and an agreement is signed with the Studebaker company whereby it can, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said a while ago, deprive the federal treasury of a sum of $2 million? They do not do that much for our manufacturers here in Canada. And this agreement with the federal government has no other purpose-it is the only one we can see-than to allow the Studebaker company to continue certain operations in the automobile field in Canada, because Studebaker cars are going off the market.
Now, we allow them to buy cars such as Volkswagens, that Volkswagen dealers could procure before and which brought 17 per cent in customs duties to the federal government, the federal treasury.
Now, we take away that 17 per cent duty from the treasury and put it into the hands of a company to enable its directors or its organization to make profits. This is not even a shadow of action in favour of the Canadian worker and the Canadian taxpayer.
And I also share the views of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). It is shameful to have allowed such a transaction or to have made such an agreement with the Studebaker company. If the minister and the

government really want to increase production and consumption in Canada, instead of allowing a company to make millions of dollars in profits, they should start by cutting taxes for the benefit of the Canadian taxpayers and citizens; the minister and the government could then say: We have truly adopted a piece of legislation or an order in council that will benefit the Canadian citizen.
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the minister is shameful because the Canadian citizens, the Canadian people are deprived of something that belongs to them. No one has the right to serve the Studebaker company at the expense of the Canadian people, and I maintain that this agreement must be cancelled. If a company no longer exists in Canada or in the United States, it should not be granted credits allowing it to import cars, which leads to some kind of dumping of those cars in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is time for the government to assume its responsibilities and, above all, for the treasury board to recognize that the interests of all Canadians and not those of any company, the Studebaker company or any other, should be the primary concern.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPORTATION OF VOLKS-WAGENS BY STUDEBAKER COMPANY
speechtext:
It seems to us that the whole purpose of the automobile agreement as explained in this house was, first of all, to assist Canada with her balance of payments problem; second, to reduce prices charged to Canadian consumers relative to prices being paid in the United States for similar automobiles

in other words to narrow the differential-and, last, to increase employment in Canada.
If there are loopholes in this agreement, or misuse of the concessions respecting import duties, which would allow a transaction of this kind to be carried out without any of the stated purposes of the agreement being fulfilled, then I think we had better take another hard look at this agreement. I suggest that both Studebaker and Volkswagen must have had some doubts whether a deal of this kind could be made under the agreement and the several orders in council, otherwise they would not have made inquiries of the Department of National Revenue with regard to it.
It seems to me that the government should have assumed responsibility, particularly in the initial stages, for ascertaining whether this transaction fulfilled one or more of the
October 27, 1966
stated purposes of the agreement. If they found that it did not assist Canada in her balance of payments position-and certainly the importation of 10,000 automobiles does not help in that respect; if they found it would not result in lower prices to consumers-and certainly the evidence before us indicates that there was no reduction in price to the consumers at all; and if it did nothing to increase employment in Canada-and surely the importation of 10,000 automobiles does nothing to enhance the prospects of a market for Canadian produced automobiles in Canada, then it seems to me the government should have advised the two companies concerned that a transaction of this kind was not in accordance with the stated purposes which the agreement and the subsequent orders in council were designed to accomplish.
I suggest, therefore, that the government should now take a long, hard second look at this agreement to block loopholes which might allow further transactions of this kind or permit other transactions which would deprive Canada and Canadians of the stated benefits of the agreement.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks on the proposed amendments to the National Housing Act. The general tenor of the minister's speech yesterday was that the position of house construction in Canada was not too bad this year. I contend that we have arrived at a very serious situation in Canada with regard to house construction. I quote, for instance, from the Monetary Times for October, 1966:
[DOT] (3:50 pm.)
Squeezed by tight money and sharply rising costs, the industry-if their press notices are to be believed-is crumbling at its foundations, and this year will build only 140,000 houses, 110,000 short of the nation's needs. Those that are being built are horrendously costly in terms of the average wage earner's capacity to pay.
The minister himself admitted that this year house construction up to the end of last month has dropped by 23 per cent. I cite the publication Home Building News, September issue, to the effect that July starts were down 27 per cent. The reference is to individual housing. I consider that the position in Canada today with regard to new house construction is similar to what it was in 1956. At that time it was practically impossible to obtain a loan for a new house. In various parts of the country, particularly in British Columbia as I am sure the minister is aware, there are widespread lay-offs in the construction industry. This results in large part from a decreasing demand, as in the United States, but also from the lack of money in Canada to provide new housing.

I realize there is not too much the minister can do by way of providing moneys from conventional sources. I think the minister should consider taking the action we took in 1957 and 1958 and make substantial amounts of government money available for direct loans. It is not good enough for the minister to say-

A suggestion might be made that the minister put that question on the order paper, or perhaps he has the answer. I will have the information available. The minister has assured us that direct loans will be available this year for the same number of houses as last year. I contend this is not good enough. Not only are there thousands of Canadians who are unable to obtain loans either directly or from conventional sources, but the shortage of housing is creating a pressure which is increasing the cost of housing. Last year alone, according to figures presented by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the cost of the average house increased by over $900. I do not have any figures for this year, but I understand that in Toronto the cost of the average house has increased by over 20 per cent so far. I feel that the minister should seriously consider making additional moneys available for direct loans.

I turn now for a moment to the question of housing for low income families. The minister takes some apparent satisfaction from the fact that some 1,100 units were built for low income families and another 555 under federal-provincial schemes, making a total so far this year of 1,600 units. In my opinion this is just a drop in a very big bucket. Figures provided by the Senate committee on aging, for instance, show that in 1961 out of 516,000 elderly families 30 per cent to 35 per cent or roughly 180,000 had difficulty in securing housing at a reasonable cost. In that same year, out of 235,000 elderly single people
117.000	had difficulty in finding housing at a reasonable cost. In 1961, therefore, some
300.000	elderly family and non-family households had difficulty in providing housing at a reasonable cost. I am not blaming the present government only. From 1946 to 1963 low dividend housing provided only 8,000 units in the whole of Canada. I contend that the government should take a serious look at the provisions of the National Housing Act and the extent to which it satisfies the tremendous need for housing of families on low incomes.
Certainly raising the interest rate from 5f per cent to 5| per cent was in my opinion completely unwarranted. This is all direct government money and does not come from conventional sources. If anything, the government should have materially dropped the interest rate applicable to money for public and low cost housing. Perhaps I am reading something sinister in the minister's speech, Mr. Chairman, but there certainly was a reference to a continuing review of the National Housing Act interest rate. I recognize that in order to encourage conventional lenders to go into the housing market there must be a satisfactory return. However, may I make a suggestion to the minister? If an increase in the National Housing Act rate is being considered, he may want to study the possibility of having a double interest rate, that is, a lower interest rate on a loan up to a certain amount and then a higher interest rate beyond that. This would tend to help those families on low incomes. This precedent has been accepted in the case of the Veterans Land Act. There is one interest rate applicable on loans up to a certain amount and then a higher interest rate applies beyond that level. The same provision applies to the Farm Credit Board. It might be advisable to consider that on loans of up to $12,000 a rate of 5.5 per cent or 6 per cent would be applicable, and then the interest rate beyond that would

be whatever the minister considered necessary to attract conventional lenders.
The minister indicated that accommodation for some 6,000 students has been provided so far this year. This is a nice figure, but it falls short of the requirements of the universities today. I have had first hand experience with the difficulties students have not only in obtaining admission to residences but in finding reasonable accommodation close to university centres. Here again, the government might consider some inducement, perhaps by way of lower interest rates, to encourage the building of student housing.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
One of the factors involved in the increase in the cost of houses is the provision of land suitable for building. The minister may not recall this specific case but I am going to refer it to him. It concerns a subdivision in the Prince George area. Incidentally, I was pleased to note that according to the minister's speech yesterday such money as is available will be allocated to certain areas where the need is greatest, and he mentioned the Prince George area where I know he recognizes the tremendous demand for new housing.
I am wondering to what extent the individual case I am going to describe now is compounding the difficulty. In this particular case Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation refused to approve the Park Ridge Heights subdivision in Prince George for N.H.A. purposes. Before we go into detailed discussion of the bill in committee perhaps the minister would have his officials advise him about this matter, because I have studied this subdivision project and I cannot see why C.M.H.C. should not approve it, particularly in view of the fact that they recently approved another subdivision outside the city which is very close to this one, as well as another one just a short time ago. The point I am trying to make is this. Here is a subdivision offering fully serviced lots at lower cost; yet C.M.H.C. refuses to approve the subdivision, thereby forcing people to buy higher-priced lots, and often lots that are not serviced, inside the city limits.
Naturally I welcome the amendment whereby N.H.A. loans will now be made available for the purchase of existing houses. This was a promise which was made by the Liberal party in 1963 and in 1965 and we welcome the belated appearance of this amendment.

May I suggest to the minister that I do not think an amount of $10,000 is going to do the job the minister has in mind, simply because the type of house that you can buy for $10,000 today in the urban areas in any event is not the type of house that should or could be salvaged. Again, Mr. Chairman, the minister might consider the suggestion I made before, that of a double interest rate to help people on lower incomes, charging say 6 per cent on the first $10,000 and on the next $5,000 to $8,000 a higher rate, one that the minister considers appropriate.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution under consideration deals with amendments to the National Housing Act.
That resolution affects a very important economic and social field, namely that of construction in Canada. Besides it is a field which has known, in the last couple of years, various fluctuations that should lead us to look for ways to improve conditions in that area.
Indeed, according to a well-known statistics firm, and according to the Southam Building Guide, the cumulative value of the construction contracts awarded in Canada during the first eight months of 1966 is more than 4 per cent lower than the record level reached last year.
I must add that the Southam Building Guide bases those statistics on approximately 52.9 per cent of the value of all construction contracts awarded in Canada, including new construction, repairs and renovation, and on almost 83 per cent of the value of new construction.
The decrease of 4 per cent in the value of construction contracts in the country during the first eight months of the year is due to various factors. One of them is the drop in the total value of contracts over $1 million awarded since the beginning of the year. The value of such contracts is in fact 8 per cent lower than in 1965.

October 27, 1966
National Housing Act
Another reason for that 4 per cent drop is the set-back in residential construction which decreased by almost 13 per cent during the first eight months of the current year compared to the same period last year.
Still another factor can be found in the engineering works which also have shown a substantial reduction of over 32 per cent.
To the three factors I have just mentioned, Mr. Chairman, one could also add indirect action or lack of positive intervention from the governments, reflected, for instance, in too heavy a tax burden, the imposition of some special taxes such as the 11 per cent tax on building materials, credit restrictions, high interest rates. Those are other reasons which contributed to that decrease of 4 per cent in the value of construction contracts in the country.
It must be recalled also that the Quebec association of housing contractors, through Mr. Fernand Boisse, president for the fiscal year 1965-66, protested quite often against the various special taxes which were harmful to the construction industry, as well as against interest rates which are too high, and I think that it even submitted to the various governments very judicious briefs on the matter.
Mr. Chairman, the housing field fits very well into the criteria of productivity about which so much is being said with respect to present economic difficulties.
It is a fact that prices are continually going up and that the increase in prices greatly exceeds the Canadian productivity rate. Now, I feel that the best way to fight inflation is to take all the necessary steps to increase Canadian productivity. Increasing Canadian productivity means encouraging production in all fields, including housing projects of all types.
And consideration is being given to implementing this restrictive policy, this behind-the-scenes policy which was started by this government about a year and a half or two years ago and which is paralysing several areas of economy with respect to housing.
If the government really wants to take the means at its disposal to fight increasing prices and inflation, it will not achieve this aim with speeches made by the hon. ministers at various banquet tables; it must take positive action and put the necessary moneys into national productivity. We must not hesitate to increase Canadian production, rather than increase taxes, restrict credit, raise the rate
IMr. Allard.]
of interest up to 6.75 per cent, measures which are responsible for the present productivity standstill and which will in no way check inflation, at least from my own standpoint in dealing with the matter.
This afternoon, I will not comment on each item in the resolution since, as I pointed out to the hon. minister, there could be other explanations and other amendments included in the bill which will probably be introduced some time next week. At that time, I intend to comment on the various provisions of the bill.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out to the house this afternoon that one of the provisions in the resolution worries me very much; it provides for encouragement by this government to student housing projects which will not be limited to university students only.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The tentacles of centralization are being extended further. It is always the same old story under our Canadian skies. Years ago, the central government, a Samson in the fields of taxation under its control, which it has repossessed and is ever so reluctant to hand back to the provinces-another example of this is found in the current federal-provincial conference-invaded the field of housing, which rightly belongs to the provinces. Why? Because, the constitution says so. I wonder what purpose that constitution now serves, Mr. Chairman.
I do not know if the hon. minister has read the 1865 debates on Confederation where legislators expressed the spirit and the letter found in the Canadian Constitution of 1867.
The hon. minister will see readily that according to those accounts it was never intended that the central government should set the pattern or control or act in the fields of construction and housing. On the contrary, all those matters of a family, social, local and regional nature, by virtue of Section 92 of the Canadian Constitution, fall under provincial jurisdiction. But it is no longer being complied with. We might as well ask all our university professors of constitutional law to pick it up and throw it in the wastebasket. Why teach our students the respective responsibilities of the central and provincial governments when the central government intervenes in the fields of education, sewers, municipalities and housing, which according to their professors are matters that come under provincial jurisdiction?
October 27. 1966

Well, the present government will have to act truly fast-it does not usually, but it might surprise us-and amend the constitution if that is the approach it intends to take in 1967. If the government wants to keep the present constitution, it should amend it; otherwise, let us have a new one. To my mind, it is absolutely ridiculous, even illusory, for us legislators in Ottawa to sit in this house, constitution in hand, debating proposed legislation. And this is not the first resolution since January 18 last.
I say that seeking to increase the number of housing projects which will not be restricted only to the accommodation of university students-for, until now, instead of handing enough money to the provincial governments, Ottawa has kept the bulk of the money here, camouflaging it in various fields to build student housing as annexes to Canadian universities. It seems to me they always act in devious ways, but extensively, probably to build all kinds of schools which the minister has not described for us. He mentioned a nursing school, a school for social groups. He did not deny that, in due course, they may build all the high schools and secondary schools in Canada. If Ottawa keeps all the money, why have provincial governments? Poor wards, poor little girls who are no longer considered intelligent enough to have the right to look after their own wardrobe. That, Mr. Chairman, reminds me of the old definition or concept of provinces at the time of the Romans, when provinces had no autonomy whatsoever. They depended exclusively on the central government in Rome in all administrative matters. That is what the present government is doing. It is changing the Canadian provinces into-

speechtext:
It is precisely this arrogant attitude, Mr. Chairman, namely that the provinces do not have to take advantage thereof if they do not want to. But we are in a field of provincial "jurisdiction" here.
National Housing Act
Why should the provinces not have the necessary funds to fulfil their obligations? Why should Ottawa pull all the strings and control all the financial levers enabling it to make propositions to the provinces under those terms with the understanding that if the provinces are not satisfied, all they have to do is refuse and then, let them shift for themselves? It is precisely this arrogant attitude that has become unacceptable within the concept of federalism. If we want to do away with federalism, if we want to return to legislative union like in 1840, towards which we seem to be drifting gradually, well then, let us be frank enough to admit it. Then the provinces will know what political and constitutional action to take, under those circumstances. Well, Mr. Chairman, I would very much like to see provisions on the matter included in the bill.
Another point overlooked by the resolution is the fact that there seems to be no provision-maybe the bill will take this fact into account, I hope it does-this government makes no provision for a single-family dwelling program at special rates. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that laws, laws and dollars are all very well, but all this must not be based solely on material considerations, mathematical and geometric calculations, left, right, north and south. The legislative measures that we adopt must be impregnated with a social, moral, human, and family philosophy.
In the field of construction, the government should give serious consideration to the plight of all Canadian family heads.
I am referring to the small wage-earners and the farmers, the small wage-earners in our large and medium-sized cities, who are not able to raise their children in complete freedom, under a roof of their own. I maintain that the head of a family in Canada has a natural right to wish for and to have a house of his own, so as to raise his family decently, free and unhindered.
The government should provide legislation for construction programs, and since it appears to enjoy trespassing into fields of provincial responsibility, it should at least include philosophical, family and social considerations in the bill to be introduced, so as to enable the family administrator to build a home at a special rate, say 5 per cent, because the present rate of interest is too high.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I would also urge the government to eliminate immediately and entirely, in its next

October 27, 1966
National Housing Act
budget, the 11 per cent tax on building materials, to help house-building contractors. If we consider the various causes of bankruptcy in Canada, we note that house-builders come in second place, after business bankruptcies. After attending their convention, and hearing their discussions, we learned that this is not simply due to bad luck or to inefficiency; in general, Mr. Chairman, the reason is that the fiscal burden is too heavy and the interest rates excessive. If we want to increase Canadian productivity, that should be abolished immediately.
A new budget will be brought in but it seems to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is planning, not to send us manna, as a snow-storm, on Christmas eve, but to increase taxes, according to his own conception of the fight against inflation, which I find altogether inacceptable. That is a personal opinion. Everyone is entitled to his opinions; that is why our constituents send us here, to express opinions.
I am of the opinion that to fight inflation, we should not pick the taxpayers' pockets; their funds are low, as it is. Look around; most Canadians in any province have not enough money to provide for their needs, but the Minister of Finance hopes to milk further people in financial straits. I do not speak of financiers and companies of whom we heard during the question period, who have just pocketed $2 million-we do not know, they are very clever people-but I speak of Canadians, three quarters of whom are family-heads, workers, farmers, office clerks. We should increase Canadian productivity, and inject in the field of construction and housing vitality instead of oppression.
Some members, whose opinions I respect, spoke in this house, namely the hon. member for St. Paul (Mr. Wahn), from Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso), from York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury), from Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), advocating the creation of a department of urban affairs and housing in the future.
That is logical, considering all the interventions and centralization which the central government, in Ottawa, not only this one but also the previous ones, have established. Imagine, Mr. Chairman, that you have, for instance, in section 92 of the constitution, paragraph 10 which gives exclusively-if the word "exclusive" still means something in the twentieth century I ask broad-minded people to understand this-to the provinces all local works and undertakings. Of course,

there are three exceptions, works like the trans-Canada highway which connects one province to another. But this is not the case in the field of local housing. You also have paragraph 13, which places under exclusive provincial jurisdiction property and civil rights in the province. If there is a field which comes within the terms of property, it is that of housing, unless I am narrowminded or unless I am from another century. We also have paragraph 16 of section 92 which gives the provinces jurisdiction over all matters of a merely local or private nature in the province.
If this government, or the one which will succeed it-it may be shortly, we do not know, for we hear more about replacing the leaders nowadays than about changing the government-wants to create a department of urban affairs and housing, as is also being mentioned in this house by some members-it would obviously follow centralization, direct and indirect intrusion upon provincial fields.
There is some talk of establishing a department of education. Well, as far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, no such department should be created, and the central government should honestly, definitely and seriously consider giving back to the provinces-for they are not satisfied, as I realized these last few days

their taxation fields instead of interfering with their responsibilities.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if one listened to the minister yesterday or read his speech in Hansard one could only reach the conclusion that any relationship between the speech and reality was accidental. From his speech one might think we were really doing a good job in the housing field and beginning to meet the needs of the people of Canada.
I do not know where the minister lives or what newspapers he reads, but one does not have to be the minister in charge of housing, or an official with all the facilities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at his disposal, to know that the facts are otherwise. One can take up the newspapers of almost any city in Canada almost any day and read case after case of people in this affluent Canada, not just in the rural areas or in the poorer provinces of the Atlantic region but in some of our wealthier cities, who are presently living in deplorable and disgraceful conditions. Of this we have heard nothing from the
October 27, 1966

October 27, 1966
National Housing Act
At 81 per cent on a 25-year term, It will cost them $135.22 per month to carry a first mortgage of $17,000.
At 10 per cent on a five-year term, the second mortgage of $5,000 will cost them an additional $105.74 per month.
The editorial goes on to deal with the cost of property taxes and so on and points out that the financing of such a house comes to a total of around $270 monthly. How many people are there in this country who can afford to make that kind of monthly payment unless they sacrifice other basic necessities? Yet, Mr. Chairman, they have no alternative.
In this context I want to use myself as an illustration, and I think I am better off than 90 per cent of the people in this country. I had no intention of buying a house in Ottawa but last month I was informed very curtly that my rent, which I thought to be fairly substantial, was going up by 10 per cent. Even at that I think I was lucky because I know of many cases here in Ottawa where people have had their rent increased by 18 per cent to 20 per cent.
If I am buying a house it is because I have no alternative, and there are tens of thousands of people who have no alternative. The government has not faced up to what is needed in this country, a housing policy which will provide houses for people in the income range of $5,000 to $8,000 a year and which will provide rental accommodation at rents which people who make less than $5,000 a year can afford.
In the Winnipeg Tribune of October 8, 1966, there appeared the first article of a series dealing with housing. It was headed, "Slums-A City's Cancer". It pointed out that several weeks prior to the appearance of the article a delegation of residents of my constituency appeared before the city council of Winnipeg complaining that their area was being turned into a slum. They had a legitimate complaint because their area is being turned into a slum.
One may ask how and why? The answer is that several years ago-we in Winnipeg were long overdue for it and deserve a great deal of criticism on that ground-we started our first urban redevelopment project. Many of the people in that project area, which is situated in the constituency of my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre, were moved into a new housing development and the others remaining had to find alternative accommodation. They moved into the area I have been talking about, and simply because

they do not have the kind of money required to keep the housing they have rented up to any kind of standard, it is becoming a slum like so much of the rest of the old part of Winnipeg.
I wish to quote a description of this area from the article in the Winnipeg Tribune, and may I say I am sure this is something which is also happening in Vancouver and possibly in the constituency of the minister who is in charge of housing.
Near the comer of Jarvis and Andrews is a huge, dilapidated yellow building that extends for nearly a city block. Its front yard is a series of muddy ruts, which run with water when it rains. Its sidewalk is chipped and broken.
According to one middle-aged woman resident, the home contains 85 people. Most of them, of course, are children-children running around in bare feet on a fall day, wading in the rain pools, knocking on doors looking for their mothers, hitting each other, and crying.
One would think that in this kind of accommodation the rents would be low, but the contrary is true. Rents are high. In the main the rents are paid by the people of Canada because the great majority of the tenants who live in this kind of slum are on welfare. They cannot work and they do not earn enough to pay rent in private housing accommodation. The city of Winnipeg cannot enforce its own health regulations because there is no alternative for these people. The city cannot put these people out on the street.
What is true of families is also true of retired people. In Winnipeg-and I give the various community organizations like the Lions, the Kiwanis and the Canadian Legion a great deal of credit for the leadership and initiative they have shown-we have built a number of housing units for elderly people. We built several hundred units, enough, according to figures I saw recently, to accommodate about 1,000 people. But the last survey made, which was four or five years ago, indicated that there was still a need for housing accommodation for 4,200 old people who are retired.
A private builder in Winnipeg recently made plans to build housing accommodations for 200 elderly people, and on the very first day he got requests from almost 1,000 people who wished to move into the units. This is what is happening in my own city of Winnipeg, and what is happening in Winnipeg is being duplicated in Vancouver, in Montreal, and the situation in Toronto is even worse. normal business operation which will be met through the methods which are workable in our free enterprise economy.

I suggest to the minister that the proposals he has now made will no more solve the problems in respect of housing in Canada than the proposals he made two years ago when the National Housing Act was amended. The housing problem will not be solved until the government realizes that it and it alone can provide a solution. If housebuilding is left to private industry houses will continue to be built only for people who can afford to buy or rent them. The housing problem will not be solved if interest rates on mortgages are allowed to be fixed on the open market. If the government means business it is obvious it will have to provide money to subsidize interest rates so that the average individual can afford to pay the rate. This may be a revolutionary idea, but I suggest there is nothing wrong with it and a great deal to be said for it. The government should provide money to subsidize interest rates. If we are going to solve the housing problem and clear out slums in this country the government must allocate a much larger amount of money-double, triple or quadruple-than it has been providing up to now.
Surely the minister knows that rental rates at this time in Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver range from $175 to $225. In order that the average individual can rent adequate premises we must in some way lower rents to $60, $65 or $70.

Let me also urge the government to establish a department of urban affairs with responsibility for meeting the housing needs of Canada. The minister of such a department would not consider this as an extra job or one which he could do in his spare time but would spend his full time and effort to find a solution to the major problems of housing, slum clearance, urban redevelopment and the provision of recreational facilities, hospitals and schools in co-operation with provincial and municipal authorities who, after all, have the major responsibility under our constitution.

people of Canada as the program he announced two years ago which has failed so signally up to now.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are called upon to study today a resolution to amend the National Housing Act. I do not think that there is in the federal statute books any legislation which over many years allowed the Canadian citizens to benefit more directly from funds put at their disposal by the federal government than the National Housing Act.
In every corner of the country, in all classes of society, there are people who can now live in a single or multiple dwelling only because the federal government, several years ago, that is in 1954, agreed to assume its responsibility with regard to loans to stimulate home ownership in Canada.
The proposed amendments cover many points. But today I would like to deal with only one amendment which will certainly be much discussed. In that respect, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) raised earlier objections, which seemed based on an interpretation of the constitution which I am far from accepting. It is true that the constitution allocates powers to the central government and to the provinces. It is true that the constitution grants to the provincial governments powers in the fields of ownership and civil rights. It is true also that the same constitution recognizes, very clearly and very definitely, the powers of the central government with regard to money and credit. But it is under those undeniable powers that the federal government extends its jurisdiction on all financial institutions which create money and credit. And that is how the federal government created a farm credit board, an industrial development bank and so many boards which spread among all Canadian citizens the benefits of bank credit. Therefore it is an undeniable power that the federal government holds under the constitution and exercises in all fields it deems appropriate.

Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that the federal government cannot use its power to create credit to impose such conditions that there would be interference in fields which do not come under its jurisdiction. But, as a matter of fact, and since the beginning, the federal agency, that is the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has always made sure to lay down conditions which applied only in the field of credit.
This is so true that the municipalities and the provinces have easily been able to establish all sorts of rules concerning housing, safety measures, and the location of those buildings on the various lots. Therefore, property rights were then entirely respected, but the federal government undoubtedly had the right to make available to the citizens the funds, money or credit necessary to reach goals which, ultimately, were those of the provinces.
We see now that co-operation in this field is essential, and it is sought increasingly. Since the member for Sherbrooke states the problem particularly with regard to Quebec, there are two extremely important sectors to which the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation intends to spread its activity. First, say in the field of urban renewal, which involves credit. This urban renewal involves also the implementation of city planning regulations, the development of new lands and so on; therefore, in these circumstances, an urban renewal policy cannot be put in effect by the federal government alone. As far as I am concerned-and this view is shared by many of my colleagues,-I am opposed to the setting up of the federal department of urban renewal, because I feel that if the federal government-and I am now taking its part-has a very definite responsibility in the field of credit to housing, it does not have, under the constitution, all the powers necessary to control an urban redevelopment. These powers belong to the provinces which might have delegated them to towns and cities. It is precisely because of that responsibility that the Quebec provincial government has set up an urban redevelopment agency long awaited, precisely to promote co-operation in that field, and to provide

especially for a use of federal funds in the province of Quebec as efficient as in the other provinces.
I know that there has been an extremely interesting and successful experience in that field of urban renewal, with the Dozois scheme in Montreal, and I know also that my colleagues from the city of Montreal, in cooperation with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation authorities, provincial authorities and Montreal municipal authorities, work very hard to develop a new project of urban renewal known as "La petite Bourgogne" project. Then, the three competent authorities, namely the federal, provincial and municipal authorities within their own field of activity, will accept to set up a joint plan or program for the renewal of that district of Montreal which greatly needs it.

Such an avenue is open to federal-provincial co-operation. It is in such a context, I believe, that the activities of the C.M.H.C. must be contemplated, that is in an atmosphere of continued co-operation with different levels of public administration connected with urban renewal.
I hope that the program to be enforced shortly in Montreal will serve as an example for other urban renewal projects in other cities of the province of Quebec. Under the pretext of false autonomism, the necessary co-operation should not be refused to federal authorities which are willing to provide assistance for the renewal of some districts in cities in such great need of financial help.
There is also a second point I should like to bring up at this time. It raises precisely the problem of jurisdictions with regard to the assistance provided for student housing projects in various fields of education in Canada. Mr. Chairman, in rising to make a few brief comments on the resolution I realize I am a fortunate Canadian because I was able many years ago to build a log cabin in the wilderness and be free of debt. I also realize that a great many Canadians who need housing at this time do not enjoy the same fortunate circumstances. I rise to express my support for the amendments suggested in the resolution as a step toward the development of an over-all housing policy that will meet the increasing needs of the Canadian people for satisfactory housing at a reasonable cost. For many years various aspects of housing have concerned my constituents. On that account, on numerous occasions I have discussed these matters and their requests with the present minister and senior officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I have no hesitation in expressing my appreciation of the prompt 23033-5811
National Housing Act
and courteous attention they have paid to any representations I have made on behalf of my constituents with respect to their problems. Naturally I recognize the fact that they are not settled to their satisfaction on all occasions, but I think both the minister and his officials did the best they could under the law and under the regulations in effect at the time.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I must say that I am delighted with the co-operative and constructive attitude of the house on this important legislation. I was very interested to hear the minister quite properly give credit to the former Progressive Conservative government for certain amendments it made to the National Housing Act, and I was interested to hear the hon. member for Kamloops rise in his seat and express his appreciation of and his support for these proposed amendments. I am one of those members in the opposition who do not believe it is the prime and essential function of the opposition on all occasions to act like a lot of fox terriers, snapping at the exposed political underwear of the government. I think it is the responsibility of the opposition to criticize as effectively as they can, and it is also their responsibility to offer alternatives. I think, Mr. Chairman, you will usually find that while the members of this group are often very caustic in their criticisms of some of the aspects of legislation introduced by the government, they try to offer alternatives which they think will be of advantage to the Canadian people.
Housing requirements of various types are rapidly increasing, first, because of the growth of our population, second, because of the development of a new concept of the social responsibility of the state with respect to housing and other measures and, third, because of the effects of related legislation that provides for university and college education and expansion and other legislation that has an effect on the demands placed upon the C.M.H.C.
I was very interested to note that the hon. member for Kamloops said that forecasts and surveys of housing units indicated the need for at least 750,000 new units by 1970 and the possibility that this figure may reach a million units by that date. In my opinion no field of human welfare indicates more strongly the urgent need for over-all planning and programming in co-operation with the provinces, the municipalities and other non-government organizations which I have found from my

October 27, 1966
National Housing Act
experience as the member for Kootenay West, are only too willing to co-operate and participate in the satisfactory administration of such programs.
Throughout the years many organizations in my riding have been interested in urban renewal surveys. The city of Rossland is very interested in a proposal to that effect and the city of Trail is now engaged in urban renewal developments much to the advantage of the city itself and of the population that will be affected. They have been interested in housing developments for their growing communities because of the expansion of industry in the area. They have been interested in low rental housing for our senior citizens, and I emphasize that this is a continuing great need. In my opinion these provisions should be applied in the following cities in the riding I have the honour to represent, in Trail, Castlegar, Nelson and Nakusp so that our senior citizens will have the opportunity to enjoy the advantage of low rental housing and yet have the advantage of being visited by the people with whom they have lived for most of their lives.
We have also been interested in the housing for students attending Notre Dame University, Selkirk college, and vocational and trade schools. I am very pleased to note that Notre Dame University is getting substantial assistance in this respect, and I trust that other educational institutions will obtain similar assistance, particularly after the passing of this amending legislation.
We have also been very interested in the particular requirements of the smaller communities which I think have been somewhat overlooked by the conventional lending institutions. It does not always pay them to send people to these communities to inspect the construction and to inspect the buildings after they are completed. Very often the local fire brigade regulations are not quite in line with what they require. I was very interested to hear the hon. member for Kamloops speak on this question because his experience, coming as he does from the interior of B.C., is very similar to mine in Kootenay West. There is a great need for further consideration of these smaller communities.
I must say I am pleased to know that the National Housing Act is to be amended so as to provide for the first time that loans may be made to persons who wish to purchase, occupy and improve existing housing. I have urged this proposal for years as I know of many well built older homes in the cities,
[Mr. Herridge.l
towns and rural communities in my constituency that can be modernized and improved with a loan such as it will be possible to obtain when this legislation is passed. I support this amendment on practical, economic and aesthetic grounds. I think it is most unfortunate to see some of these houses that were built many years ago falling apart. I am glad to hear that the $200 million available under the act for university housing projects is to be raised to $350 million. This is a very necessary amendment and I predict that this sum will have to be increased in the very near future because of the great expansion of university, college and vocational school education, the increasing number of students and the need for housing for these students.
I am glad that this legislation will provide for an additional three year period within which the construction of a sewage treatment project must be completed if the municipality concerned is to be forgiven payment of a part of the principal of the loan and of the accrued interest. I am sure this amendment will be of assistance particularly to the smaller municipalities. I am also glad that the limit in section 22 of the National Housing Act is to be raised from $3.25 billion to $4 billion for direct lending and that the increase will be used for the purchase and improvement of existing houses and, as the minister indicated, possibly for another 31,500 direct loans next year. I now have a few suggestions to make. I do not want to speak at great length, but first of all I wish to say that there is a great need for the development of co-operative over-all planning among the federal and provincial governments, the municipalities, and the nongovernmental organizations which are willing to participate. I suggest that there is nothing like getting the participation of local people in programs and getting their understanding, whether it is in the field of housing, in the field of ARDA, or other projects that may be

undertaken by federal-provincial co-operation.
I suggest there is a need for a lowering of the interest rate. I think that is one of the reasons that housing has been lagging in Canada. According to a study made by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, Canada is lagging in housing. In 1963 Canada spent only 3.6 per cent of its gross national product on residential construction, ranking eleventh among 15 countries. In 1953 we ranked fifth in residential construction. In 1963 we were ninth in housing completions per capita and over the 10 year period, 1953-1963, we had the slowest proportional increase in housing completion of any country. I do not think we can be proud of that record when we look at the advantages we enjoy in respect of natural resources, industrial equipment and so on.

In my opinion and in the opinion of other members of this party, this has been influenced to a great extent by high interest rates. In that connection I should like to quote briefly from an editorial in the Toronto Star for Wednesday, October 26, a newspaper which I understand normally supports the Liberal party:
Ottawa's tight money scourges the weak.
The tight money policy of the federal government is ruthlessly denying people a chance to get decent family housing.
In the Metro area, interest rates on conventional first mortgages have crept as high as 8J per cent in some cases. Rates on second mortgages commonly range from 9 to 11 per cent.
Consider what this means to a family without savings seeking an average price ($22,000) older house to buy.
Then the editorial goes on to deal with the amount of interest to be paid, the property taxes to be paid, and reads as follows:
Since housing authorities say it is unwise to spend more than 27 per cent of family income on housing, this family would need an income of $1,000 a month or $12,000 a year in order to comfortably afford that average house.
The article concludes with this paragraph:
There is something viciously wrong with a monetary policy that denies families housing at prices and rents they can afford, while allowing commercial construction to proceed full blast.
I agree with that.
And there is something wrong with the social conscience of a government

I would say the social conscience of all of us.
-that will lean so heavily on tight money to fight inflation, disregarding the human consequences.
National Housing Act
It may bring in national contributory pensions. It may (tardily) raise old age security payments to those in need. It may promise medicare for the 'nth time.
But the government shows a callous heart when it shuts the door to shelter on middle and low income people unless they can pay usurious interest rates.
How many Canadian families must sacrifice their comfort, peace of mind, and decent living standards to the demands of "sound" money?
I recognize that the minister personally is not directly responsible for fiscal policy or for high interest rates, but in my opinion there is something more necessary. I believe that every family should have decent housing and should be entitled to the privacy that goes with a decent home. Every person in the home is entitled to live in a house that provides the privacy of having a room to oneself. This is necessary for the proper development of personality within a democracy.
I believe that housing is also lagging because of the tremendous increase in real estate values. I have seen this happen in the constituency I have the honour to represent. I might refer to a little village within six miles of where my home is at the moment. When I came to the house you could buy a lot 25 feet by 115 feet in that village for $25. At the present time these lots are selling for no less than $1,250. A person who is going to build a home requires at least four of these lots under these circumstances. This imposes an added burden on those who wish to build houses. I am wondering if the minister could give some consideration to a scheme for the purchase of land along the lines of that undertaken by the Veterans Land Act administration some years ago? Under this scheme land was purchased well ahead of immediate requirements.
I was going to Vancouver recently and I listened to two men who were talking in the lounge car of the train. One of them was a very prominent supporter of the Social Credit government in British Columbia. He came from Kelowna. He had heard about a housing development taking place around Kelowna. He offered a farmer $20,000 for a 30-acre farm on the outskirts of Kelowna. Evidently he had advance notice of this housing development. He said he had sold five quarter acre lots, I think, for $4,000 each so he had already obtained the return of his capital. I think the federal and provincial governments must exercise some judgment with respect to possible housing developments and the land

required, not just next month or next year but even 10 or 15 years from now. In this way speculation at the expense of those who can least afford it could be prevented.
As I have said before, I believe further consideration should be given to the needs of smaller communities because they have been overlooked by conventional lenders. I usually try to speak from experience, so I mention again in the little village of Nakusp which is about six miles from my home. There are some persons in that village who borrowed money under the auspices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at a time when the village was unincorporated. The village has since been incorporated, so people can borrow from the corporation as the former builders did although there is no sewage system and septic tanks have to be used. The community is on a sandy bar overlooking the lake, so there is no difficulty about that. The people in adjacent communities, in which houses costing up to $25,000 are being built, are not permitted to borrow under the auspices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation because they are adjacent. The corporation gives these loans to the old community, although adjacent communities situated on benches of land 100 to 250 feet higher than the main community are not permitted to borrow from the corporation.
I suggest that the minister give some consideration to such situations and to the needs of these smaller communities, not necessarily to farmers living on farms but to those who wish to live in smaller communities and commute to their employment. There is a lot of that around Trail, Nelson and the little village of Nakusp which I used as an illustration.
As I said before, I feel we must get the participation of the non-government organizations in all these communities. I give the corporation credit for what it has done in this respect. Some of the officials of the corporation have gone to various meetings of chambers of commerce, labour organizations, farmers institutes and farm organizations to explain the act and its operation. I suggest that further efforts should be made in this direction to give adequate information and publicity to the vast problems of housing and problems related to housing. This can be done through the press and periodicals as well as by the distribution of literature through the corporation.

I give the corporation credit for publishing some very informative literature on the various aspects of housing, types of housing, the possibilities under the act and the interpretation of the act. I suggest that even that program should be stepped up and that wherever possible officials of the corporation should be sent to these regions to take advantage of the opportunity to inform local organizations, which means informing the local people, of the problems involved. We could seek their co-operation in making this act a success. In this way, within a few years we will have a housing policy in Canada, as the result of over-all planning between all levels of government and participation by non-government organizations, that will provide the housing so necessary for the Canadian people at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I want to say: Three cheers for federal intrusions in housing.

I have listened with great interest to the debate between the Quebec members on the constitution and the federal role in housing. I rather liked the speech of the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane. Without getting into the constitutional argument may I say that had it not been for the benefits of the National Housing Act over many years we would have far fewer houses in Canada than we have at the present time. It may be argued that this field is primarily a provincial responsibility, but the provinces just would not have done the job. I think of this too in connection with the conference on university financing. Our universities would have far fewer buildings today had the federal government not taken an interest. The provinces just did not do the job.

October 27, 1966
National Housing Act
Other speakers have made reference to the name "Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation". They have said they would prefer the corporation to be called the department of housing or the department of housing and urban affairs. This is not a new idea. Others have suggested it in the past and I too should like to see this done. I suppose the reason for the present title is the sensitivity of the federal government to the use of the word "housing" in the light of the provincial responsibility. The fact remains that the corporation is involved in housing and in urban redevelopment and I believe that notwithstanding some provincial objections the body should be renamed and called the department of housing.
I support the remarks made by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North who suggested that housing and redevelopment activities are sufficiently important to justify the setting up of a separate department under a separate minister. I cast no reflection on the present minister, but he has other very important things to do and I suggest his primary portfolio as Minister of Labour is big enough without the added responsibility of housing matters.
Many speakers have pointed out during this debate that there is a severe housing shortage. Everybody knows it. We have had a housing shortage ever since the second world war because we have never caught up with the demand. At this particular time the situation in our larger metropolitan centres is serious. Maybe it is in some of the smaller ones; I do not know. The minister mentioned that the number of housing starts had not fallen to the extent he had anticipated. However, the fact that there has been a decrease is serious enough.
It seems to me that family formations must be increasing in numbers at this time, though I do not have figures with me at the moment to prove this contention. At any rate, the number of births, the increase in school enrolments and so on all indicate this to be a fact. Yet at a time when more families are being formed the supply of housing is declining. I should like to illustrate the shortage of housing by a quotation from the Vancouver Sun of October 8, 1966. I am sure the minister has read it but I put it on record because it illustrates the seriousness of the situation. The article is by Moira Farrow and it reads:
Some get mad, some allege discrimination and some break down and cry.
This is how people are reacting to the citywide shortage of rental accommodation' for low and middle-income families.

[DOT] (5:50 pjn.)
It is a shortage which has gone from serious to critical in the last three or four months, according to housing authorities.
City planning director Bill Graham said Thursday there is little the city can do to relieve the shortage.
"I suspect the situation will be with us for some time," said Graham. "It has been brought about by tight money."
The gravity of the problem was underlined by a Sun poll of several city rental agencies.
They also blamed partly the tight money situation, which they said has put a brake on construction.
And they said increasing population and demolition of many old houses have contributed to the problem.	1
None of the agencies could see any immediate solution.
"We have desperate people phoning us every day," said Margaret Barker of H. A. Roberts Ltd.
She, like all the other agency spokesmen, said the greatest shortage is of unfurnished houses renting between $100 and $150 a month.
John Murphy of Ker and Ker Ltd. said some people claim when they cannot find accommodation to rent that they are being discriminated against because they have children.
Some people did comment that the proposed legislation to allow loans on existing homes would help the situation, but I am sure the minister and the officials of the corporation are well aware of the existing shortage which is very serious for many families. As the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich mentioned this afternoon, these new loans will have an effect on the existing supply of houses, and rents surely are going up for apartment accommodation and for individual homes.
The minister said that direct loans increased last year but loans from other sources decreased, and that is not good enough. I think one remark in the minister's speech yesterday illustrates the attitude of the government to the question of housing. As recorded on page 9132 of Hansard the minister said:
The fact remains that, as I have said, every dollar is at a premium from the standpoint of investment. Perhaps that is not surprising because in a free enterprise economy money generally goes where the rewards are the greatest, and it is difficult for anyone who favours a free enterprise economy and a political philosophy based on free enterprise to be too critical of the efforts of our investors to channel their funds into areas where they will get the best interest rates, so long as these rates are not usurious or are not unreasonable.
Farther on he said:
I think I should make it clear that the government intends to pursue the course it has been following, but it is not our intention to pick up all of the slack that has resulted from the substantial withdrawal by private lenders from the residential field.
October 27, 1966	COMMONS
If the federal and provincial governments are not going to take up the slack, then who is going to do it? As the minister has said, private investors will invest their money where it will bring the greatest return and we cannot stop that. But if the vital need for housing is to be met the job can only be done by government or it will not be done at all.
It is unfortunate that the minister seems satisfied that the government has increased direct loans. That is commendable, but it needs to do a great deal more. From all the indications and opinions in the business pages of the newspapers by people in the investment world, this situation is going to continue for some time, and so it will require the government to act, to move in and supply the money to meet the housing needs of the Canadian people.
I also think it is very unfortunate that a certain amount of really unnecessary construction work is taking place at the present time. I know the federal government cannot control all these things. Building permits and so on are the concern of provincial and municipal governments. But it is a fact that at a time when money is scarce, when building tradesmen are scarce and when, as we are told, materials are scarce, we have shopping centres going up in cities that already have an abundance of them. I hope some of the provincial governments will give attention to that matter because all the materials and labour being used could be utilized to increase the stock of housing in Canada. I also hope the minister will give more thought to this problem.
As I said a few minutes ago, there is no apparent end within the next year or so to the money supply problem. It is evident that the amount of money coming from private sources is going to continue to be in short supply. Therefore houses will not be built unless action is taken by the federal government through C.M.H.C. by supplying funds and encouraging provincial governments to do the same. If such action is not taken then the very serious problem being faced by many families throughout the country will continue for quite some time.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Nicholson thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-241, to amend the National Housing Act, 1954.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to delay the estimates of this department. However, as you probably know, I am

vitally interested in the operation of the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement and its effect upon my constituents in particular. The results so far in the Niagara peninsula are far from satisfactory and there is a great deal of concern for the future. I was one of the many who wholeheartedly endorsed this auto pact. It is true that more jobs have been created in the automotive industry, but at the same time there have been extensive lay-offs and many more workers may be displaced as a direct or indirect result of the Canada-U.S. auto pact.
I feel the government should take a stronger stand to see that the intent of the agreement is carried out, not only by labour but by management. In order to strengthen the government's position priority should be given to setting up a government-labour-management committee which would deal with specific problems in the auto plants as they arise.
As an example of how this committee would work, may I speak of the situation that exists in the Niagara peninsula at the present time. At the moment there is a severe lay-off at the McKinnon plant of General Motors in St. Catharines. At Hayes Steel Products in Thorold South, just a few miles away, there is under construction a new automotive frame plant which should be into production next April. Both situations are the direct result of the automotive trade agreement. Is it, then, not practical and moral that priority of employment at Hayes Steel should be given to the dislocated workers at General Motors?
Another industry, Conroy Manufacturing Company, has recently been purchased by Kelsey Wheel Corporation, and other than knowledge of the purchase the workers at Conroy's have no assurance of continuation of work. Obviously this causes a great deal of concern with workers who have spent their working lives at Conroy's and are established in St. Catharines. If the government-labour-management committee were functioning, these fears could be alleviated.
It would appear to me, from personal observation, that there has been some lack of co-operation by management in supplying the federal government with the necessary information that would be required to have advance notice of major changes in the levels of employment in order to minimize the effects of dislocation. I believe it should be mandatory for all companies concerned to supply such information when requested by our government.
October 27, 1966

[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
Another area where there seems to be lack of co-operation is in the utilization of the supplemental unemployment benefit plan, commonly abbreviated and called SUB or
S.	U.B., instead of the transitional assistance benefit program, commonly called TAB or
T.	A.B. This plan is for workers displaced as a result of the trade pact. In 1955, after a prolonged strike at General Motors, the
U.	A.W. was successful in establishing the S.U.B. program on a 5 cents per hour basis. This 5 cents per hour was in lieu of an increase in wages; in other words it was considered part of the wage increase that U.A.W. could have had to build the SUB fund. The moneys for the SUB program are put into a central fund for each company; that is to say, all of General Motors in Canada have the one SUB fund. On this basis it would be possible for workers displaced by the trade pact to use up the fund and as a result take away from other employees of the same company who would not be affected by the trade pact. Using General Motors, our major auto industry, as an example, displaced workers in Windsor, Oshawa and St. Catharines could use up the fund, and the workers in the London diesel plant and in the Frigidaire plant of General Motors in Toronto who are not affected by the trade pact would lose their benefits. It seems to me that the use of SUB is unfair and unjust in that workers are paying for their own dislocation, and in fact some workers who are not affected by the trade pact are paying for dislocated workers.
In conclusion I should like to say that the major auto companies are not contributing to TAB. As we all know, this was not the original intention since it was expected that the automobile companies would be prepared to contribute an equivalent amount to general revenue and TAB would be paid to their employees when laid off as a result of the auto pact.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the government should, in the very near future, either ask the companies concerned to contribute to TAB or to the general fund, as they are morally obliged to do, or else the government should consider reimbursing the SUB fund and give the employees affected the benefit of the difference which may exist between their payments from SUB and from TAB.

Mr. Chairman, while neither I nor my colleagues are in favour of taking too
