long in the resumed debate on Item No. 1, several things have happened since we last discussed this item, I think in June, which in my opinion deserve some comment at this time.
The first point I wish to make derives from the unfortunate railway strike which took place in this country and the steps which this parliament was forced to take to end it. Of course I am not going to discuss that at all, but views on railway negotiations which have held for some time have been confirmed and reinforced, that the ordinary labour negotiation and conciliation machinery is not adequate to deal with the railway industry in particular, and probably with the transportation industry in general. I suggest that we should not wait until another crisis comes upon us before we take steps to improve the machinery applicable to that industry. I think the reasons why the ordinary machinery is not adequate are obvious. The railway industry in particular and the transportation industry in general constitute such a basic industry in the country that serious difficulties necessarily arise in bargaining.
I woud like to suggest to the minister that he and his colleagues in the government give serious consideration to the enactment of a railway labour act or a transportation labour act-depending on whether you want to limit it to the railways or take in other transportation facilities of the industry which come under federal jurisdiction-to provide special machinery which would deal more adequately with disputes in that area of our economy. Lest there be any misunderstanding about this I should like to emphasize that I do not have in mind the provision of compulsory arbitration. During the debate on the act which returned the railway employees to work I said-and the other day I said it to a conference of labour leaders of the Canadian Labour Congress-that it seems to me all of us including the labour leaders, must appreciate that it is not always possible to strike for as long as the labour partner in the dispute may like. Situations may arise where the interests of society require that a strike be ended before damage which might be irreparable is done.
However, I have always said-and I say it again in order that no misunderstanding may arise-that this does not justify the enactment of compulsory arbitration, because in my view not only would that derogate from the democratic process of collective bargaining but, aside from theoretical reasons and

October 27, 19S6
Supply-Labour
reasons of principle, there is a simple and practical reason why general compulsory arbitration would be unfortunate and undesirable. The reason is that in all cases where statutory compulsory arbitration is in effect the process of collective bargaining dies. If you know that at the end of the line you will have to go before an arbitrator anyway, then you simply drag your feet, and usually management drags its feet until it gets to the arbitrator.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? While I understand that he said he is opposed on principle to compulsory arbitration legislation of a general nature, is he not suggesting that some type of binding solution should be incorporated in the labour transportation legislation which he is suggesting? subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
No, I am not, Mr. Chairman. If I may continue perhaps it will become clear to the minister what my view is. It is not theory but a fact that railway unions and management

assuming there were, as there has not been, genuine collective bargaining and assuming that management were ready, as in the past it has not been, to make offers about which the unions could argue-can in most cases reach an agreement, as is the case with the overwhelming majority of labour disputes. I do not have to tell the minister, as he knows it better than I do, that the strikes get the headlines, but that in his office literally thousands of collective agreements are arrived at, the majority of which do not require conciliation; and in the cases where conciliation is resorted to this process produces an amicable settlement. Despite all the hysteria and panic that some of the pundits have aroused in Canada, the fact is that over the years, the number of strikes related to labour disputes and negotiations in this country has been relatively small. I think that in the long run everyone concerned, labour, management and government should, on the whole, be proud of the record of Canadian labour management relations. This year happened to be a bad one in one or two important areas, and as a result the minister's distinguished grey hair became more distinguished and more grey. However, this has been an exception, not a rule, and I therefore think it would be a mistake in principle, because it derogates from the freedom of the parties to negotiate, and a mistake in practical terms, to have a general law imposing compulsory arbitration.

[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
The point I am making is that you deal with situations which such as the railway strike which are extraordinarily sensitive, and impose extraordinary considerations, but you deal with them as they arise and you hope they will not arise often. What I have in mind is a separate transport labour act which will provide particular machinery for bargaining, for conciliation and mediation, so that you will have in your Department of Labour, as a result of such a statute, people trained in the railway industry, who can get into the job of conciliation or mediation early. I have in mind the provision of tighter time limits, so you do not have the embittering experience of giving notice of bargaining in November, 1965 and not coming down to the wire until August, 1966.
Everyone who has studied the history of labour negotiations in the past 12 months, as I am sure the minister has, knows quite well that if real negotiations had gone ahead last February or March the likelihood is that a settlement would have been made without a strike. There are various reasons for this statement and I do not wish to go into them. Since the bargaining went into August, with all the things that happened in between in the country, to the economy, to profits and all the rest, the situation became much worse. Most important of all, the situation became a lot worse because the rank and file of workers were becoming bitter and frustrated after ten months of endless negotiations and conciliation during which the employer made no offer so far as money was concerned.
What I have in mind is a special statute providing different steps for negotiation which would bring experts into the picture early. I hope the Department of Labour would have qualified experts who would be paid sufficient to make them proud of having the job and giving their expertise to the railway industry, as well as to other labour-management problems. They would come into the picture early. They would not have to wait to be invited. They would be at the doorstep of the parties when they started negotiations and, wherever possible, would guide them away from the collision course when it appeared likely that is where they were headed.
I suggest also such an act would provide not only more effective conciliation procedures, but also more effective mediation procedures, so that men like Mr. Carl Gold-enberg, could come into the picture before
Oclober 27, 1966

the last minute, after a strike has already been in existence. I suggest that even in the last case-although perhaps because of the circumstances it might not have worked-we might have been able to avoid a strike had a mediator with his qualifications been in the picture last January, February or March before the situation heated up to the point where a strike became inevitable.
I have not worked out all the details of such a statute. However, I know many of the minister's advisers and I have the greatest respect for them. I am sure the minister can get a great deal more help from them. I am not suggesting this statute could be written overnight. It would probably take a good many months of study to make it effective. What I am saying is that, obviously, over the years the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act has been found wanting so far as the railway and transportation industry generally is concerned; that the time has come to produce a separate statute, as they have in the United States in the railway labour act, containing separate provisions to deal with railway disputes.
The second point I want to deal with briefly has also become more acute since last June. I refer to the use of injunctions in labour disputes. I appreciate that this question falls largely within provincial jurisdiction, but you will forgive me, Mr. Chairman, if I make a few general remarks before making one or two specific recommendations. I happen to hold the view, and I make no apology for stating it as frankly and clearly as I can, that injunctions have no place in labour disputes. I am referring to injunctions of any kind, not merely ex parte injunctions.
As a member of the bar of the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario, it is my duty, Mr. Chairman, to point out that what I am about to say is said without any disrespect to the bench or any member of the bench. Having said that, it is my experience that injunctions are strike breaking weapons. They are used by management for the purpose of breaking a strike. I think this is totally wrong. It is totally wrong under any democratic system of justice that the courts should be in a position where they may be used by management for strike breaking purposes. This is what has happened.
I noticed, according to the press the other day, that at a recent Liberal meeting in Ottawa the Minister without Portfolio referred to this matter. You will be relieved, Mr. Chairman, to know that I am not going
Supply-Labour
to speak about that meeting tonight. As I have said, I noticed that at a recent Liberal meeting in Ottawa the Minister without Portfolio fathered or mothered or promoted some labour resolutions, one of which concerned the abolition of ex parte injuctions. Of course I agree with him. If he were here I would invite him to get to his feet and join with me right here in parliament in repeating what I understand he promoted at the meeting of his party. I may say however that getting rid of ex parte injunctions does not meet the situation. Even if the other party gets 48 hours notice, as I understand the situation would be under Ontario procedure and also in some other provinces so far as I can remember their procedure, that does not help you. The problem relates to the fact that injunctions can be obtained at all, and particularly in the way in which they are obtained. They are obtained, as I am sure every member of this house, lawyer and non-lawyer knows, on affidavit evidence. The affidavits are prepared by the solicitor for management and have some relationship to the way in which witnesses would give evidence if they were called to the witness box. But affidavit evidence is not in fact the same.
It takes time to read the affidavits and more time if you are going to cross-examine the deponent. Then it takes even more days if you are going to file any affidavits, and reply will need still more days. In the meantime an injunction will almost certainly have been issued, because the only way you can deal with the application for an injunction is to go into court on the day the motion is, as we lawyers call it, returnable and get an adjournment. You get it, certainly, on condition that the injunction is in force in the meantime. By the time you have completed your cross-examination, and you have filed your own affidavits, and your deponents have been cross-examined by the other side, the strike may be broken by the injunction.
Furthermore it seems to me to be totally wrong, and always has seemed so, that a matter as important as a labour dispute should be solved on the basis of somebody writing an affidavit, instead of people who make the charges being there to defend them, to give evidence by word of mouth, and to be subject to cross-examination in court at an open trial.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Although I must preface my remarks again by expressing the respect I hold for the

Supply-Labour
courts of Canada, I find that the most reprehensible part of these injunctions-and this was the reason there was trouble at Tilco and at Lenkurt in British Columbia-is that they prohibit from picketing not only the people against whom there is some evidence of unlawful acts, but they prohibit everyone from picketing. A typical injunction will commence in a way something like this: "Defendants" -A, B, C, and D-who presumably are alleged to have committed some unlawful acts, "their agents, their servants and any persons who know of the order", and so on. I am not giving you the precise legal jargon but that is the effect of it.
Now, Mr. Chairman, usually the order is published in the papers. The employers make sure that it also is announced over the radio and sometimes on television, and it is put up in public places in the form of a poster. There is hardly a person in the community who is likely to be unaware that an order has been made and unaware of its general purport. So even if I accept the proposition that there may be three, four, five, six or even ten people who have committed unlawful acts on the picket line, and even if I were to agree that these people should be enjoined, it seems to me totally unreasonable in the administration of justice that not only those who are alleged to have committed unlawful acts are enjoined, but everybody else is enjoined from demonstrating his solidarity with the persons on strike and picketing.
In the result, Mr. Chairman, ordinary law-abiding Canadian workers or Canadian union representatives are now in jail in Peterborough and on the west coast, some of them having been sentenced to 15 days, to two months, three months, four months and as many as six months because of the demonstrations they have made.
It is extremely difficult to deal with this situation. In my opinion the labour movement is justly determined to continue its agitation, and if necessary its defiance; ready to take the consequences of so doing, until the law relating to injunctions in this country is amended.
One does not have to go very far, Mr. Chairman, to see how it can be done much more properly. In the United States in the thirties, I think it was, the Congress there passed the Norris-LaGuardia Act. I appreciate that in the United States the federal system is different from that in Canada, but I merely want to refer to the situation there as an

illustration. Certain aspects of that act should be introduced into Canadian law across the country, namely, that you cannot obtain an injunction on affidavits; it can only be obtained after a hearing in open court, with witnesses giving evidence in direct examination and being cross-examined.
There are areas, Mr. Chairman, where you cannot get an injunction at all. In addition, the injunction obtained can enjoin only those who the evidence proves have violated the law. It cannot enjoin those who are innocent of such violation, and that is what we ought to aim at.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that this is a provincial rather than a federal matter as far as its general aspect is concerned. But in one aspect is is federal, and that is this: It is possible for this parliament to amend section 366 (2) of the Criminal Code, which is what is known as the exculpatory section, so that the watching and besetting which is permitted under section 366 is defined in such a way as to discourage the courts from limiting the number of pickets and from descending upon pickets and upon unions because they were attempting to persuade people to support them.
On a previous occasion, Mr. Chairman, I made this appeal to this house and I make it again. I urge the minister as Minister of Labour to discuss with his colleagues the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General whether it is not possible to amend section 366 (2) so as to provide three things. The first one is that the pickets are allowed to be as numerous as they like as long as they behave peacefully and within the law.
Since when in this land do we prohibit peaceful demonstrations? Yet every court I have been before first of all limited the number of pickets to two, three or four at one entrance because that was enough to convey information. The whole morale of the strikers is destroyed by that act of the court, which is to the benefit of the employer and to the detriment of the striking employees. Therefore I say that section 366 of the Criminal Code should specifically provide that picketing is permitted singly or in small or large numbers, so long as the participants picket peacefully.
Second, Mr. Chairman, the section ought to be amended to provide that the picketing is permitted to be carried on not only for the
October 27, 1966

purpose of obtaining or communicating information, as is provided by the present subsection, but in addition it ought clearly to provide that the picketers have the right to persuade or to attempt to persuade employees, customers, clients or other persons to abstain from doing something, so long as their attempt to persuade them and their persuasion is carried out in a lawful manner.
After all, Mr. Chairman, this is the object of picketing. It is sheer nonsense to say that the picket line is there only to convey or to obtain information. Indeed it is sheer hypocrisy to insist that that is so, because it is not so and it never has been so. The picket is there to protect his job. He is there to try to persuade other people, whether they be employees, customers or clients of his employer, not to cross the picket line, so that his strike will pinch his employer as much as possible and produce a settlement. Strikes are unfortunate, Mr. Chairman. Each time they occur every one of us regrets it, including the strikers. But when they do occur the strikers have the right to be given the opportunity to picket in a proper way, and not to be limited and confined, as is the case at present, by injunctions.
I suggest that this amendment to section 366 (2) of the Criminal Code is necessary, because from my knowledge of the law over the years courts have interpreted picketing by reference to section 366 (2) of the Code, or its predecessor section.
Third, Mr. Chairman, not only should the striking employees themselves be permitted to picket, but anybody else who wants to support them and who wants to demonstrate on their behalf should be given the right to do so. If this parliament were to make that change in the Criminal Code it would be the first important step toward encouraging the courts- and it is within the power of this parliament to do this-not to issue the kind of injunction order that has resulted in the unfortunate arrests and prison sentences imposed recently. In my humble opinion and with all respect to the judges who imposed the sentences they are completely out of all reason to the alleged violations. If an otherwise law-abiding organizer of a union has to spend six months in jail because he dared demonstrate in the face of a court order against him, the court is placed in a position of arrogance rather than importance. It endangers the respect which people feel for the courts and for the administration of justice. Those who think that by imposing such
Supply-Labour
severe sentences the people will be deterred from what they are doing, make a very grave and profound psychological mistake.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
The likelihood is that the savagery-and this is not too strong a word in my opinion-of these sentences will increase the bitterness and resentment, and will encourage more people rather than fewer people to defy the law. This parliament can make its contribution through the amendment to the Criminal Code to which I refer.
I wish to make a third point which we have been promoting and propagating for a long time, and which I have suggested on many occasions. I noticed the other day, that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration raised the same point in a speech. If I understand correctly, my leader asked a question about this speech by the hon. minister, and the minister made it clear that he was expressing his own opinion only. I invite the minister to express his opinion in parliament. Here it would count more than on an outside platform.
I suggest that when employees, which as a group are certified to bargain collectively under the law and after going through all the procedures and processes required by the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, go out on a lawful strike, the employer should be prevented by law from hiring strikebreakers. The whole concept of the strike, itself an unfortunate breakdown in normal civilized relationships, is that the strikers on the one hand suffer loss of income and the employer on the other hand is hurt by loss of business. My point is that in this confrontation if there were no strikebreakers, the parties involved would get together sooner rather than later. Both parties would more easily come to their senses, arrive at a compromise, the workers would resume work and the employer would make profits again. But if, as the law now provides, you permit employers to hire other workers who were not there before the strike, only the poor strikers are hurt.
As some hon. members know, I was involved in one of the landmark cases in labour law in this country. The Royal York Hotel was on strike, and the Canadian Pacific was involved. I will not bore members of the committee with details, but I refer to it to make my point. During the strike the Royal York Hotel fired the employees. I took the

October 27, 1966
Supply-Labour
position on behalf of the union at that time that the hotel by firing the employees was violating the law because the provincial labour relations act, and the federal Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act provide very clearly that in a lawful strike an employee retains the status of employee. The Canadian Pacific took the case to the Supreme Court of Canada. I was delighted to win at every stage of the superior courts, though we had lost in the magistrate's court. But we won in the High Court of Ontario, in the Court of Appeal and in the Supreme Court of Canada.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I thank hon. members. I shall not be long.
The point I wish to make is that when we won that case we really had not won anything, because all we had was a sort of judicial declaration that the employees could not be fired. There was nothing in the law preventing the Royal York Hotel from hiring anybody it pleased. When the strike was ended there was no guarantee that the employees who had been on strike would be taken back. This therefore shows a hole in the law. We made a useful and progressive provision in our law across Canada when we said that people on lawful strike shall remain employees of the employer.
I urge the minister to give serious consideration to amending the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act as it relates to those industries over which parliament has jurisdiction. It would be an important landmark if parliament could take the next step and provide not only that a person remains an employee while on strike, which is in accordance with the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, but that he who cannot be dismissed by the employer while on a lawful strike cannot be replaced. That is, the employer should not have the right to replace

the employees who are on strike. If you do that, all the bitterness, injunctions and violence which occasionally occur would disappear. You would put the employees who are on strike and the employer on an equal balance of inconvenience when there is talk of injunctions, and you make possible the resolution of strikes, unfortunate as they are when they occur, on a much better basis.
I remind members of the committee-and I am concluding my remarks with this-that nowadays an employee does not have merely his job at stake in a strike. He has a whole range of fringe benefits and equities that he has worked up during the course of his employment. He has seniority, which is important to him. He will have a pension plan, a health and welfare plan, and an insurance plan and all sorts of benefits that affect him and his family. If he loses his job he loses more than his work, because he loses all the equity he has acquired by his years of service. That, to my mind, justifies the sort of amendment to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act I have suggested.
I thought the present was an appropriate time to say a few words on the subjects I have dealt with. I again thank hon. members for giving me an extra two or three minutes.

At this time, Mr. Chairman, I want to ask some questions regarding the right to strike in essential services, and regarding the use of compulsory arbitration. I do not ask these questions to embarrass labour or because I am anti-union. I ask them because the public asks them, because my constituents ask them, and for this reason I think they should be raised in the house.
I am not an expert in labour matters, as is the hon. member who spoke before me. I speak as a backbencher. I do not speak on behalf of my party. It may well be that labour representatives have good answers to these questions. If so, there should be no objection to the questions being asked. We are not here to favour any one group in society, but to protect and promote the public interest.
During the past two years there have been several strikes in essential services, and on several occasions governments, both federal and provincial, have resorted to compulsory arbitration to settle these strikes.
October 27, 1966

[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
On each occasion the Canadian Labour Congress and other unions have strongly condemned this action. On the other hand governments have used this procedure reluctantly and only as a last resort. In the two recent cases subject to federal jurisdiction, special legislation was enacted and the government stated that no precedent was being established. However, the public have been asking the following questions. First, why are strikes allowed at all in essential public services such as railroads, post offices, hospitals, and so on? Second, why is compulsory arbitration so bad if it is the only alternative to a strike which often seriously affects the national public interest? Third, why would the workers prefer a long strike to a quick settlement determined by an independent tribunal? Do they really gain more from a settlement after a long strike than from a quick settlement resulting from the use of compulsory arbitration? The Canadian Labour Congress often states that it is opposed to compulsory arbitration on the grounds that it is anti-union and that it is anti-democratic. But its spokesmen rarely attempt to explain why it is antiunion or why it is anti-democratic. What reason is there for believing that compulsory arbitration would be more favourable to management than to labour? Have there been any studies made of compulsory arbitration decisions to indicate which side those decisions favour in the long term? I do not know. My purpose in raising this point is merely to seek information on a point which is, I believe, of interest. Some might suggest that compulsory arbitration is wrong because it removes the right of the parties concerned to bargain freely and arrive at agreements without interference. But, Mr. Chairman, such a right has been taken from the parties directly concerned in other fields, and the solution has been accepted as being a reasonable one. When government or another public body is forced to expropriate private property and the parties concerned cannot agree on a price, the matter is referred to an expropriation board or to a court for decision.
Few people would be prepared to accept a situation where the property owner could hold out and prevent expropriation taking place until a price satisfactory to him was agreed upon. We accept the fact that the public interest must be served and that a definite decision must be taken so that work may proceed.
Supply-Labour
Those who oppose compulsory arbitration often argue that if we are to have control over wages by this process, then we should also have some control over prices and profits. Well, Mr. Chairman, the only type of compulsory arbitration I have in mind relates to such essential services as railroads, the post office, the seaway, hospitals, and so on, and in each case a certain control over rates and prices does exist. In some cases these services are public utilities whose rates must be approved by boards and commissions. In others they are government services or crown corporations financed by taxes or charging rates subject to government control. Suppose the government decides to increase postal rates or hospital rates or school taxes. The public may have the opportunity to make respresentations, but once the decision is taken people do not have the right or freedom to avoid the rates or taxes because they do not find them acceptable.
I should like to raise some further questions which are being asked by the public. There are those who say it is undemocratic to interfere with the right to strike. But I would ask whether all union members have full democratic rights within their unions. I refer to the closed shop, the check-off, the payment of union funds to political parties, the right to elect national officers or to fire them, the right to determine their salaries, the right to determine union dues, and the right to a secret ballot in deciding whether or not to strike, together with other important matters.
I listened with interest to what was said by the hon. member for York South who told us that in certain extreme instances he would favour compulsory arbitration, but that he did not think the matter should be the subject of legislation. He said he did not believe it should be the subject of legislation because once it was, there would be no genuine collective bargaining. Mr. Chairman, over the years there have been several examples of compulsory arbitration affecting the railway unions, yet in the periods between, collective agreements have been freely reached after negotiation. It would seem to me that unless there are good reasons to the contrary there should be provision, as an alternative, for compulsory arbitration in disputes involving essential services.
I believe that such a provision should be in existence so that it would not be necessary to ask parliament to pass special legislation each time there is a threat to our national interest. However, as I said when I began, I am not an

October 27, 1966
Supply-Labour
expert and I am ready to listen to the answers to these questions. It may well be that the procedures within the unions to which I referred a few moments ago are necessary if the union movement is to survive, though they are seemingly undemocratic. This may be so, but they do constitute, none the less, a whittling away of traditional democratic rights; to some extent they impose restrictions on the freedom of the workers. And if some restriction of freedom within the labour movement is necessary for the good of the labour movement, then it might well be that for the common good of the entire country some restriction will have to be placed on the right to strike.
I ask these questions not because I am anti-labour or anti-union. I do not come from the establishment or from business or from the ownership class. In asking these questions I am not trying to serve business or corporate interests, or even the government interest; in having this matter discussed in the house the only interest I wish to serve is the public interest and the interest of my constituents.
Discussion of these issues would also, I feel, serve the interests of the rank and file of union members. I have raised these questions. I should like to see them discussed openly and publicly. If there are good arguments against the procedures I have mentioned I should like to hear them. But I do not want to hear cliches and stereotype answers.

Mr. Chairman, during discussion of the Department of Labour estimates, I would like to refer to a problem which recently came to light in Quebec and which, I believe, concerns a great majority of the Quebec workers and all the Quebec members sitting in this house.
This concerns recent decisions taken by the Canada Labour Relations Board concerning the freedom of Canadian workers to choose their own union, their own negotiating unit and their own representation unit. Two days ago, the chairman and secretary general of the Confederation of National Trade Unions, the C.N.T.U., along with several directors and labour leaders concerned with the problem I am referring to, came to Ottawa to meet with the Quebec members of all parties and protest against certain decisions recently handed down by the Canada Labour Relations Board, and as well as urge us to draw up legislation to have the Canada [Mr. Allmand.J	|	,
Labour Relations Board reconsider those decisions.
That day, we received briefs from the C.N.T.U. entitled: To Quebec ministers and federal members, with reference to the problem being discussed today.
I would like to make a few comments with regard to these notes and ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) to take the necessary action to correct the existing situation along the lines of the brief submitted to us by the C.N.T.U.
We find in that brief:
That BoardMeaning the Canada Labour Relations Board.
-is made up of a chairman, appointed by the governor general in council, four management representatives and four labour representatives. Among the four labour representatives, three are appointed directly or indirectly by the Canadian Labour Congress (C.L.C.) and the fourth by the C.N.T.U.
When an inter-union dispute arises between a C.L.C. affiliate and a C.N.T.U. affiliate, it is not exaggerated to repeat what has already been written, namely "that the dice are loaded against the C.N.T.U." This becomes obvious when the decision would result in changes in allegiance of other groups of workers or when the decision is one of principle, which would have the same effects.
And now here are the facts.
The C.N.T.U. applies for union recognition to the Canada Labour Relations Board on behalf of a group of employees of the C.B.C. French network. That request is rejected on the pretext that a national unit cannot be broken up and that the application of the C.N.T.U. covers only a local unit.
Well, Mr. Chairman, in the case which we are now concerned with, the employees involved, that is those of the C.B.C., were dissatisfied with their union known as I.A.T.S.E. and which includes theatre and film employees, and they made it known through a referendum.
Here is what the C.N.T.U. brief says about it, and I quote:
Quebec workers chose to join a new union affiliated to the C.N.T.U.
The latter submits its request to the Canada Labour Relations Board and what happens? That legitimate, normal and logical request of Canadian workers is turned down.
The brief further states:
With the support of the C.L.C. labour members, the Labour Relations Board turned down the request, setting forth as a principle that when workers are represented by a "national unit", they cannot get rid of it.
October 27, 1966

Now, how is the membership of the Canada Labour Relations Board made up? As I said earlier, there are four labour representatives, three of whom are directly or indirectly appointed by the C.L.C., and the fourth by the C.N.T.U.
Mr. Chairman, how can you expect a union such as the C.N.T.U., to obtain justice when it has a lone representative sitting on the Canada Labour Relations Board while its rival union, the Canadian Labour Congress, has three? Obviously, when a vote is taken, three votes are cast against one; the three members appointed by the Congress vote according to their interests, while the C.N.T.U. representative votes according to those of his own union. Inevitably, where there are conflicting interests between unions, the C.L.C. gets the upper hand due to a larger representation. That is what happens and that is why the matter is serious, for the Quebec workers suffer the consequences of this situation. That is being done with complete disregard for the freedom of choice of his union by the Quebec worker, for his freedom to choose the representation and negotiation unit.
Mr. Chairman, we can only protest against that and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) must remedy the situation.
Needless to say that the decision taken by the Canada Labour Relations Board, was greeted with strong protest by the Quebec citizen in general as well as by the Quebec workers.
I will now quote in that respect another paragraph of the C.N.T.U. brief:
It is known that the C.B.C. employees in Quebec are dissatisfied with their labour structures: they would like to be able to exercise their freedom of choice: they are prevented from doing so by a legal body, as if the labour structures could thus be arbitrated and especially by people interested in their being "mummified".
It can be appreciated that the strong protest which arose in the province of Quebec was justified following the decision taken by the Canada Labour Relations Board. The brief adds and I quote:
More recently, the petition of recognition of the workers at the Angus shops in Montreal was rejected for the same reason, even though the wording of the decision does not say so.
Since the first decision rendered in the C.B.C. case, another union affiliated to the C.L.C. has been able to recruit the majority of the members in the IATSE local-
Supply-Labour
-representing C.B.C. employees who wished to join the C.N.T.U.-
-by taking advantage of the discouragement of the employees, telling them positively that the C.N.T.U. formula was excellent but that it would not be successful.
Yet, during that time, the problem was clearly put forward to the federal cabinet which formed an ad hoc committee to hear the C.N.T.U. as well as the C.L.C.
That ad hoc committee, formed at the beginning of April 1966 and presided by Hon. Robert Winters, heard the case of the C.N.T.U. on the 21st of the same month, and that of the C.L.C. on June 15- and we are now at the end of October, without any news. If it was intended to form a committee of ministers to save time, we hardly needed to appear.
On two occasions, we forwarded telegrams requesting that the work of the committee be speeded up; we did get acknowledgements from some ministers, but that was all. One could be led to believe that the matter of freedom is of little interest to the members and the chairman of the committee.
Mr. Chairman, what I would like to know from the Minister of Labour is when this ad hoc committee will report on its inquiry into the problem raised by the Confederation of National Trade Unions.
I see the Minister of Labour is talking with a government member. I suggest he would be better off listening to the questions we put to him, in our consideration of the estimates of his department.

In an article published, in the Monday January 24, 1966 edition of Le Devoir following a decision made by the C.J.R.B., Mr. Jean-Marc Leger wrote the following lines:
As a result, for a Crown corporation (or any other federal agency under federal jurisdiction as regards labour relations), constituting legally and administratively a sole entity, there should be, as regards every class of its employees, a corresponding sole "bargaining unit", namely a single union, on a national scale.
The board has always rejected the notion of labour plurality on the regional basis in the same sphere of action.
Settling, when necessary, conflicts of jurisdiction between labour unions with very similar aims, it clung obstinately to the thesis of the Pan-Canadian unit of negotiation, feeling that it did not have to take into account the differences, often considerable, in the working conditions from one region to another or of the socio-cultural differentiation factors. And Mr. Jean-Marc L6ger adds a little further:
But there is such a thing as law and jurisprudence, on the one hand, common sense and, on the other, justice. Through the interpretation given by the C.L.R.B., the notion of negotiation unit is liable to maintain existing situations to the benefit of the oldest or more powerful, favour a certain hardened labour unionism, disregard often important differences in the working conditions in various regions as well as the various socio-cultural characteristics, and finally deny, in practice, the right of free association and free labour affiliation.
That is what Mr. Jean-Marc Leger wrote in Le Devoir on Monday, January 24, 1966, following a decision by the Canada Labour Relations Board.

In spite of a speech from the throne full of great plans and of a vote which saved the government Friday night, it is obvious, if one opens a weekend newspaper, that the Labour Relations Board stole the limelight from us by taking a serious decision, which might have dire repercussions and could soon become famous.
And the hon. member adds a little further:
The only reason given by the board to justify its decision is that the national negotiation unit should be maintained and that there is no valid reason for setting up regional negotiation units.
At first sight, such a decision may seem sensible, even if it has a very legalistic character. In fact it is liable to worsen labour relations considerably. For the first time, the tensions which exist between Ottawa and Quebec are reflected in a field which those problems did not reach much, that of labour.
And the hon. member for Montreal-Hoch-elaga adds this:
Second, the board which made the ruling should be considered. How is its membership made up? POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-MONTREAL-REPORTED THEFT OF MAIL FROM AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in participating in this particular adjournment debate is to ask some questions that I think a great many Canadian citizens are asking relative to one aspect of the general operations and administration of our post office services across this land.
DEBATES	9217
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I do not refer to the question of insignia for our mail trucks and mail bags, which is a controversial subject these days. My concern on this occasion is with the security measures in effect at the various major airports in this country where mail is in transit. This concern is fed for a great many Canadians by the recent theft of an estimated half a million dollars worth of cash and securities from the mail room of the Montreal international airport; and before that by the theft of some $350,000 worth of gold bullion from the Winnipeg international airport. The Winnipeg theft took place last March and the Montreal theft took place just two weeks ago, on October 13.
I first asked in this house, in the afternoon of October 13, whether the Postmaster General was in a position to cast any light on that morning's theft at all. I wondered whether he could tell us how the thieves accomplished their feat and if he had any progress to report in the investigation into the crime and the hunt for the criminals. I am still interested today in those same questions; but with them I would link a further question now. I would ask the Postmaster General what steps, if any, are being taken at the major airports across Canada to guarantee there will be no recurrence of this year's Winnipeg and Montreal airport thefts where the mail is concerned.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
It is true that the Winnipeg theft did not involve mail. It involved gold bullion in transit by air and armored car. But the fact that it occured at a major airport, where tons of mail are in daily transit, added to the fact that the Montreal airport theft followed it by only a few months and did involve mail, is sufficient reason for Canadians to ask their Post Office Department to tell them just how safe their mail is.
Add to this the fact that both raids-both the Winnipeg theft and the Montreal theft -were carried out in what appeared to be almost unbelievable simplicity, under the very noses of people whom one would expect to be security conscious, and you have a situation, sir, which I suggest is deserving of the closest public scrutiny.
The question arises: If $500,000 worth of mail can be stolen, with apparent ease, from the Montreal airport, and $350,000 worth of gold can be stolen, again with apparent ease, from the Winnipeg airport, how safe is the
October 27. 1966
9218	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion mail today in Winnipeg, in Montreal, in Vancouver and in every airport in this country?
According to my information, the raid two weeks ago in Montreal was so precocious as to be almost incredible. Perhaps the Postmaster General has more substantial information on this, but newspaper reports said the thieves cut their way into a screened security area at the airport's post office building and made off with their haul while postal employees were having breakfast next door. The time of the raid was fixed at somewhere between 4 a.m. and 4.45 a.m. on October 13, while 35 of the 36 post office workers on duty at the time were taking a meal break. The 36th man, a supervisor, remained in the post office building while the other 35 men went to eat. Apparently, he neither heard nor noticed anything as the thieves gained entry and made off with the mail.
There is no reason, according to investigating officers, to entertain any suspicions of complicity in the burglary, either on the part of that man or any of the others on duty in the post office building at the time. And it is certainly not my intention to suggest that there was any element of complicity whatever.
But I ask, as I believe a great many Canadians are asking, what is the Post Office Department doing about this particular burglary, and what is it doing to ensure that mail will be properly protected at our airports in the future.
It is not good enough to say it was just one of those things, and it will not happen again. It has happened before. There was a major robbery at Montreal International Airport less than two years ago-in December of 1964-when five armed bandits tied up four workers and escaped with $115,000 worth of gold bullion, watches and drugs. What many people want to know is: what precautions are being taken to ensure that in the future our mail will be safe?
According to the Montreal district postmaster, no guards are stationed in the post office building at the Montreal International Airport because it is against the department's policy to employ armed guards. I wonder if the Postmaster General, in replying to the other questions I have asked, would tell the house also whether he is giving any consideration to a possible change in this policy in the future.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-MONTREAL-REPORTED THEFT OF MAIL FROM AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand the concern and even the curiosity which may have prompted the member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Sherman) to put his question.
I am aware that all Canadians who use the postal service every day as an essential service are anxious to know to what extent parcels, letters and money can be sent safely through the mails. I must add that on this point, the Canadian Postal Service record is rather enviable.
With regard to the theft at the Dorval airport post office, I cannot, of course, provide more information than what appeared in the press. I am sure the member for Winnipeg South will agree with me, because if the information we now have were made known, it would be most prejudicial to the investigators who are now trying to throw light on that theft.
I can assure the hon. member that the R.C.M.P. in Dorval and the investigators of the Post Office Department are conducting a very thorough investigation, in order to discover the culprits.
As for the exact amount of money stolen, I do not feel it is in the public interest to disclose the amounts we handle daily, because it would encourage further unfortunate incidents as the one which occurred in Dorval.
As far as the security in our post offices is concerned, I can assure the hon. member that the department is constantly looking into this matter, but it must be realized that even though we alter and improve our security methods in our post offices, well, thieves also become smarter and more efficient. I can assure the hon. member that the department strives as much as possible to provide an adequate protection for our parcel posts.

maintopic: EXPO '67-PASSENGER TRAFFIC FROM SEAWAY PORTS IN FOREIGN SHIPS
EXPO '67-PASSENGER TRAFFIC FROM SEAWAY PORTS IN FOREIGN SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to an amendment made in the year 1964, section 671 of the Canada Shipping Act, chapter 29, R.S.C. 1952, provided under clause
2	that no ship other than a British ship would transport passengers from one place in Canada to another place in Canada, either directly or by way of a foreign port.

By the 1964 amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, which was assented to on the 18th day of March, 1965, there was added to section 671 an amendment (2a) which in clause (b) provided that in future no passengers shall be transported by water either directly or by way of a foreign port in any ship other than a Canadian ship from one place in Canada to another place in Canada, both of which places are situated within the area comprising the great lakes, their connecting and tributary waters and the St. Lawrence and its tributary waters, as far seaward as two straight lines drawn from the north and south shores of the St. Lawrence to points on Anticosti island.
Thus, not only foreign ships, but formerly privileged British ships are effectively prevented from picking up Canadian passengers in our seaway ports and disembarking them at other Canadian seaway ports. This means that the citizens of seaway ports such as the port of Toronto, with its very cosmopolitan make-up, are deprived of the privilege of becoming paying passengers on other than Canadian ships, unless they are going abroad or to the United States.
This means that in our centennial year of 1967, due to a critical lack of Canadian passenger vessels on our seaway waters, that Toronto and other citizens will not have the opportunity to journey to Montreal by boat through the lovely stretches of the thousand islands, the St. Lawrence and the other tributaries and lakes of the great lakes system.
Mr. Harvey Currell, assistant city editor of the Toronto Telegram, on Saturday, October 22 last, writes about the trip by ship that Canadians cannot make from Toronto harbour through the seaway to Montreal's and Canada's Expo '67. He says:
From Toronto's front door, the world's greatest inland waterway stretches through the St. Lawrence thousand islands, down the six seaway locks and on to Canada's east coast.
Average Canadians aren't allowed to sail it.
No Canadian passenger ships except short-hop ferry services are left on the St. Lawrence or great lakes. The outdated Canada Shipping Act forbids foreign and even British vessels from carrying passengers between Canadian ports.
That's why you can't go down to Toronto harbour, board one of the many European freighters that also possess passenger accommodation and sail down the seaway to Montreal, Expo and Quebec.
Parliament meant well when it passed the original passenger sections of the Canada Shipping Act. They were intended to protect Canadian passenger ship lines against foreign competition in our own waters. Now, however, there isn't anything to protect. Last fall, the last two Canadian passenger services weighed their last anchors and called it a day.
October 27, 19G6

Mr. Speaker, there is only one way to quickly remedy this situation in time for Expo '67 and in time for owners of foreign vessels to make their plans for 1967, and it is urgent that the remedy be applied forthwith, because many details would have to be taken care of before next May, to be of any benefit in the centennial year and to Expo '67.
Section 673 of the Canada Shipping Act provides that the governor in council by order in council may suspend the coasting laws in Part XIII of the Canada Shipping Act, for any period specified in the order in council, in any specified waters in Canada in relation to any specified ships of any foreign country.
Section 671, which bars British and foreign ships, is one of the coasting laws under Part XIII of the act. Thus, Mr. Speaker, I am most anxious to have the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) initiate as soon as possible, if he will, and if the obstacles are not too great, the obtaining of a suspension order in council for the year 1967 that would permit suitable British and foreign vessels docking at our seaway ports, to transport paying passengers between such ports and particularly between them and Montreal.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
I understand that in addition to there being no Canadian passenger boats in service along the seaway there are only a few Canadian freighters that have paying passenger service. From my discussions with various constituents I know that in Toronto there are many
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion citizens whose origins are from abroad and who would like to travel to Montreal in 1967 in ships flying the flag of their native land. In Toronto we have people from all over the world, and in Toronto harbour we now have ships from all over the world during the seaway season. I submit that it would be helpful to Expo and interesting to the Canadian public to have section 671 suspended for the year 1967 as a trial measure. If this step were taken by the Minister of Transport at once, it would still be in time. It would be a step that would capture the imagination of Canadians, advertise and benefit Expo and warm the hearts of immigrants to Canada from all over the world.
